lec06kp04-u01-p12-bridge.text: conv2d is named convolution but correlates. In one sentence for the whole unit: what does the flip change?

lec06kp04-u01-p12-nf-lec06-kp04-p12-1.name: fig:lec06-kp04-p12|Top: 1-D convolution (x*w)[t]=Σ x[τ]w[t−τ], example [14,17]; 1-D cross-correlation (x⋆w)[t]=Σ x[t+m]w[m], example [13,19]; (x⋆w̃)[t]=(x*w)[t+k−1], example [14,17]. steps.label: Conv vs. corr
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate. Made from the confirmed lecture lec06-kp04: the pages were planned first, each page is mainly one native infographic, and terms are defined on the page where they are used. 12 main pages for a 25-minute class, plus 2 extension pages (commutativity, exercises) that are not timed. Content marked Added is not in the course source and was added by the lecture. The exercise page gives hints only, no answers.

steps.label: Weighted sum
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP04. Prerequisites: the sliding window of KP03, which multiplies the Prewitt kernel with the image cell by cell and adds up; a weighted sum, where each number is multiplied by a weight and everything is added; and backpropagation from Chapter 3, which lets the numbers of a kernel be learned from data. This lesson uses the smallest example: the 1-D signal x is 2, 1, 3, three cells, and the kernel w is 4, 5, two weights. A kernel, also called a filter, is a fixed set of weights. Lay the kernel on the signal, multiply the aligned cells and add: that is one output; move the kernel one cell to the right and compute again. The kernel must lie fully inside the signal, so there are only 3 minus 2 plus 1, that is 2 positions; this is the valid output, and in general a signal of length n with a kernel of length k has n minus k plus 1 of them. The right side shows the question: at the same position, laying the kernel down as it is gives 2 times 4 plus 1 times 5, which is 13; flipping it first gives 2 times 5 plus 1 times 4, which is 14. The numbers differ. An analogy: the theory is like a pancake, flipped before it is pressed; the code is like a rubber stamp, stamped directly. The analogy covers only the direction of the kernel. Next, the next page covers the subscript of convolution.

steps.label: Subscript
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the weighted sum. Signal-processing textbooks define 1-D discrete convolution: x convolved with w at position t equals the sum over tau from minus infinity to infinity of x of tau times w of t minus tau. Tau is the summation index: it sweeps every input cell and is not the output position t; cells outside the signal and the kernel count as 0. The key is the subscript t minus tau. Look at the three axes: the first is the kernel as given, 4 at 0 and 5 at 1; the second is w of minus tau, where the minus sign mirrors the kernel, so 5 moves to minus 1 and 4 stays at 0; the third is w of 1 minus tau, where adding t equal to 1 moves the mirrored kernel to position 1, so 5 is at 0 and 4 at 1, exactly the flipped 5, 4. So the indices of convolution subtract, and the kernel is flipped before it slides. Flipping the kernel means reversing its order: 4, 5 becomes 5, 4. Next, the next page covers the full convolution worked out.

steps.label: Full convolution
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the subscript of convolution. Substitute the main example, x equal to 2, 1, 3 and w equal to 4, 5, into the definition term by term, for t from 0 to 3. This computation was added by the lecture, hence the Added chip. Every row is the flipped kernel 5, 4 moved to position t. At t equal to 0 only x of 0 times w of 0 remains: 2 times 4 is 8. At t equal to 1: 2 times 5 plus 1 times 4 is 14. At t equal to 2: 1 times 5 plus 3 times 4 is 17. At t equal to 3: 3 times 5 is 15. Listing every position where kernel and signal overlap in at least one cell gives the full convolution, n plus k minus 1, that is 4 numbers: 8, 14, 17, 15. At t equal to 0 and 3 one cell of the kernel hangs outside the signal, drawn faint; only at t equal to 1 and 2 does the kernel lie fully inside, so the valid output is 14, 17, n minus k plus 1, that is 2 numbers. In the row t equal to 1, x of 0 is multiplied by w of 1, which is 5, and x of 1 by w of 0, which is 4: the kernel was flipped to 5, 4 before it was aligned. Next, the next page covers cross-correlation.

steps.label: Cross-correlation
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the full convolution. Code usually skips the flip. The operation that lays the kernel down without flipping is cross-correlation, written with a star: x cross-correlated with w at t equals the sum over m from 0 to k minus 1 of x of t plus m times w of m. Here the indices add: w of 0 always lines up with x of t and w of 1 with x of t plus 1, so the order of the kernel is kept, and the orange 4 always comes first. t runs from 0 to n minus k, which is exactly the valid output. With the main example: at t equal to 0, 2 times 4 plus 1 times 5 is 13; at t equal to 1, 1 times 4 plus 3 times 5 is 19. Cross-correlation gives 13, 19 and convolution gives 14, 17: the same x and w, really different numbers. A common error is to read w of t minus tau as w of tau minus t and slide the kernel as it is; that computes cross-correlation. Next, the next page covers flipping makes them equal.

steps.label: Flip and they match
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on cross-correlation. This is the key page of the unit. All three columns use the same signal 2, 1, 3; orange is 4 and blue is 5. The left column is convolution: the kernel is already flipped to 5, 4 and, following the definition, labelled t equal to 1 and 2; it gives 14, 17. The middle column is cross-correlation with the original 4, 5 and gives 13, 19. The right column is cross-correlation again, but with the flipped kernel w tilde equal to 5, 4: 2 times 5 plus 1 times 4 is 14 and 1 times 5 plus 3 times 4 is 17, exactly the left column. In general, let w tilde of m be w of k minus 1 minus m, which flips the kernel; then x cross-correlated with w tilde at t equals x convolved with w at t plus k minus 1. The k minus 1 on the right is only a shift of numbering: the valid output of convolution is numbered from k minus 1 and that of cross-correlation from 0. Here k is 2, so t equal to 1, 2 of convolution correspond to t equal to 0, 1 of cross-correlation. The multiply-and-add skeleton is the same; only the direction of the kernel differs. Next, the next page covers flipping twice in 2-D.

steps.label: Flip twice in 2-D
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on flipping makes them equal. An image has two directions, height and width, so the kernel K is 2-D too. 2-D convolution: I convolved with K at i, j equals the sum over p and q of I of p, q times K of i minus p, j minus q. p and q are summation indices that sweep the image, and i, j is the output position. Both subscripts subtract, so the kernel is flipped once along the rows and once along the columns. Look at this 3 by 3 kernel with the numbers 1 to 9 in order, shaded from light to dark. Flip left-right: the first row becomes 3, 2, 1. Then flip up-down: the first row becomes 9, 8, 7 and the last row 3, 2, 1. Together this is a 180-degree rotation: the 1 at the top left moves to the bottom right and the 9 at the bottom right to the top left. As a formula, K tilde of m, n equals K of k minus 1 minus m, k minus 1 minus n, where m, n sweep the kernel cells and k is the side of the kernel, here 3. Next, the next page covers a 2-D cross-correlation worked out.

steps.label: 2-D correlation
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on flipping twice in 2-D. 2-D cross-correlation does not flip the kernel; it puts the kernel's top-left corner at i, j of the image: s of i, j equals I cross-correlated with K at i, j, the sum over m and n from 0 to k minus 1 of I of i plus m, j plus n times K of m, n. This is the corrected form of the source formula. The output s is called a feature map, and s of i, j is its value at position i, j. Example: the 3 by 3 image I has rows 1, 2, 0; 1, 1, 2; 0, 1, 1, and the kernel K is the 2 by 2 identity, 1 on the diagonal and 0 elsewhere. The output size is 3 minus 2 plus 1 times 3 minus 2 plus 1, that is 2 by 2. Take s of 0, 1: the yellow frame covers rows 0 and 1 and columns 1 and 2, holding 2, 0, 1, 2. Multiply cell by cell and add: 2 times 1 plus 0 times 0 plus 1 times 0 plus 2 times 1 is 4. The other three cells work the same way, and the output rows are 2, 4 and 2, 2. Next, the next page covers the symmetric kernel and the numbering.

steps.label: Symmetric kernel
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the 2-D worked example. This example hides a trap. The identity rotated by 180 degrees is itself, K tilde equals K, so convolution also gives 2, 4 and 2, 2. When the kernel does not change under rotation, the two operations agree; to see a difference you need a kernel that changes, which is left for Exercise 3. The right side is a relation added by the lecture, hence the Added chip. As in 1-D, cross-correlation with the flipped kernel is convolution up to a shift of numbering by k minus 1: I cross-correlated with K tilde at i, j equals I convolved with K at i plus k minus 1, j plus k minus 1. By the definition of convolution, the full convolution sits at i, j from 0 to 3, and the valid output is the middle block, starting at i, j equal to k minus 1, which is 1. Renumbering that block from 0 gives the cross-correlation s. Whenever the lecture writes the valid output of convolution, it means this renumbered version. Next, the next page covers the same set of functions.

steps.label: Same functions
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the symmetric kernel. The key is that the kernel of a convolutional network is not written by hand but learned by backpropagation. We already saw that convolution with K and cross-correlation with K tilde give exactly the same output. Every kernel on the left pairs with its flip on the right, with the same output: convolution with 4, 5 and cross-correlation with 5, 4 both give 14, 17; convolution with 5, 4 and cross-correlation with 4, 5 both give 13, 19. So all convolution networks and all cross-correlation networks are the same set of functions; only the arrangement of the same numbers differs. Because the two sets are identical, the expressive power is the same; expressive power means all the functions a kind of network can represent. Gradient descent only adjusts the kernel numbers downhill on the loss and searches this set for one with a small loss; it does not care what the convention is called, so it finds one without the flip too. Think of writing with the left or the right hand: with enough practice both write well. The analogy only says the results are equally good; the kernels the two conventions learn are flips of each other. Next, the next page covers when the flip matters.

steps.label: When flip matters
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the same set of functions. The argument of the previous page has one assumption: the numbers of the kernel are learned. In two cases the flip matters. First, the kernel is a fixed, hand-designed filter, such as the horizontal Prewitt kernel of KP03 with rows 1, 1, 1; 0, 0, 0; minus 1, minus 1, minus 1. Rotate it by 180 degrees and every sign reverses: it becomes minus H, the blue positives and red negatives swap, and the detected edges change sign too. Exercise 2 lets you check this on a small patch; the answer is not given here. Second, a case added by the lecture: weights trained in one framework are moved into code that uses the other convention. Then the kernel must be rotated by 180 degrees first, otherwise the output is wrong. Next, the next page covers the names in code.

steps.label: Names in code
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on when the flip matters. Connection to code. PyTorch's torch.nn.functional.conv2d and TensorFlow's tf.nn.conv2d are called convolution but compute cross-correlation, without the flip. The NumPy case was added by the lecture, hence the Added chips: np.convolve flips the kernel and is true convolution; np.correlate does not flip and is cross-correlation. The lecture's program uses these two functions to check the earlier numbers. Papers often write the asterisk of convolution, while the code mostly computes cross-correlation. At this point the sliding multiply-and-add has an exact formula. But the same multiply-and-add can also be written as one huge fully connected layer. Compared with a fully connected layer, what does convolution save? That is the topic of KP05. Next, the next page covers the summary and misconceptions.

steps.label: Summary
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the names in code. One-sentence summary: convolution in theory flips the kernel before sliding; deep-learning code usually does not flip and actually computes cross-correlation. Flipping only rearranges the kernel's numbers, so the two forms have the same expressive power, and since the kernel is learned, training works without the flip. The top row shows 1-D convolution, 1-D cross-correlation and the flip relation, with main-example results 14, 17; 13, 19; and 14, 17. The bottom rows are four common misconceptions. One: the kernel must be rotated by 180 degrees or the network cannot train; wrong, it trains without the flip and learns the flipped kernel. Two: the summation index on the right is the output; wrong, it only sweeps the cells. Three: a function named conv2d computes true convolution; wrong, it mostly computes cross-correlation. Four: one example agreed, so the two are the same; wrong, they agree only when the kernel is unchanged by rotation, like the identity. Next, the next page covers the extension on commutativity.

steps.label: Extension: commute
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the summary. This is an extension page, not timed, and it needs some background in signals and systems. Convolution is commutative, swapping the operands keeps the result: the full convolutions x with w and w with x are both 8, 14, 17, 15. Cross-correlation in general is not. The full cross-correlation below was added by the lecture, hence the Added chip: like the full convolution, it lists every position where kernel and signal overlap, with zeros outside the signal, t from minus the quantity k minus 1 up to n minus 1. In the main example, x cross-correlated with w is 10, 13, 19, 12; treating the longer x as the kernel, w cross-correlated with x is 12, 19, 13, 10, the order reversed. In the Fourier domain convolution is pointwise multiplication, while cross-correlation needs an extra complex conjugate. These properties matter in signal processing but do not affect a convolutional network that learns its kernel. Next, the next page covers the extension exercises.

steps.label: Extension: exercises
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on commutativity. This is an extension page, not timed. All four exercises give hints only; compute first, then check with np.convolve and np.correlate. Exercise 1: x is 1, 0, 2 and w is 3, 4; compute the valid outputs of convolution and of cross-correlation; the hint is that convolution first flips the kernel to 4, 3. Exercise 2 was added by the lecture: a 3 by 3 patch with the horizontal Prewitt kernel; compare the signs of the two operations; the hint is to rotate the kernel by 180 degrees first. Exercise 3: use the earlier image I with the kernel K of rows 1, 2 and 0, 0; this kernel changes under rotation, so the two operations differ; the hint is that the rotated kernel has rows 0, 0 and 2, 1. Exercise 4 was also added by the lecture: the signal 3, 1, 4, 1, 5 with two kernels of length 3; think about which kernel is the same before and after flipping. That ends KP04; the next unit, KP05, covers sparse connectivity and parameter sharing.
